\subsection{Benchmark Datasets}

Ten public datasets were evaluated: five regression and five binary classification tasks (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), with 180 to 7,584 observations and 18 to 316 groups. Sleepstudy and ChickWeight retain smaller samples of 180 and 578 observations, respectively; the other eight datasets have at least 919 observations. The dataset set was revised after examining an earlier evaluation: Machines, Oxboys, Loblolly, Aids2 and Males were replaced by MathAchieve, Spruce, Radon, Contraception and Exam. This selection was exploratory, partly informed by earlier sample-size and performance limitations, rather than a prespecified representative sample of prediction tasks. All reported tables use the revised dataset set.

\input{datasets_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

\paragraph{Regression}
Sleepstudy predicts reaction time in milliseconds from Days, with subject-specific intercepts and slopes. ChickWeight predicts weight in grams from Time and categorical Diet, with chick intercepts. MathAchieve predicts mathematics achievement score from SES, MEANSES, Minority and Sex, with school-level random intercepts; this is a classic hierarchical linear model benchmark with 160 schools. Spruce predicts log stem volume from days of growth, with tree-specific intercepts and slopes; Occasion is not supplied to any method. Radon predicts log indoor radon concentration from basement indicator and county-level uranium, with county random intercepts; this is a canonical multilevel benchmark with 85 counties.

\paragraph{Classification}
Contraception predicts contraceptive use from age, number of living children and urban indicator, grouped by district (60 districts). Toenail predicts the recorded ``moderate or severe'' outcome from treatment, time and visit number, grouped by patient (294 patients, repeated measures). VerbAgg predicts the dichotomized response from Anger, Gender, behavior type, situation and mode, grouped by respondent. Train predicts choice1 from the two alternatives' price, time, changes and comfort, grouped by respondent; the choice identifier is excluded. Exam predicts whether the normalized exam score exceeds zero (normexam $> 0$) from individual and school-average prior attainment, school gender composition, verbal reasoning band, intake band and sex, grouped by school (65 schools). This fixed threshold is not a sample-median split. These outcomes and model predictors have no missing values in the downloaded versions.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}

\subsubsection{Two Prediction Regimes}

\textbf{Regime A: within-group observation holdout.} A random 25\% of observations, rounded down with a minimum of one, is held out separately within each group having at least two observations. At least one observation remains for every tested group. Singleton groups remain training-only. This evaluates prediction for known groups using their fitted information; it does not evaluate prospective forecasting beyond the observed time range.

\textbf{Regime B: out-of-group holdout.} A random 25\% of complete groups, rounded down with a minimum of one, is held out. No labeled support from these groups is available. TabMixNN uses zero random effects, and the classical mixed model uses its fixed part. For nonlinear models these are plug-in predictions at zero latent effects, not marginal integration over new-group variation. Kinship/GP extrapolation is not evaluated in this suite.

The primary tables use split seed 20261015, shared by all methods. A fixed sensitivity extension repeats both regimes with split seeds 20261016, 20261017, 20261018 and 20261019, keeping the model configurations and all three neural initialization seeds unchanged. These additional splits were specified after inspecting the primary analysis and are reported as an exploratory robustness analysis, not independent confirmatory validation. Within each reported split, test outcomes do not enter model fitting, adaptation or preprocessing. All categorical coding and numeric/target standardization are fitted on the training partition. Unseen categorical levels receive the training reference coding. The recorded split manifests permit exact reconstruction.

\subsubsection{Models and Training Budgets}

TabMixNN uses one hidden layer of width 32, embedding dimension 8, UN covariance and a Gaussian or binomial head. Each fit uses 2,000 full-batch Adam updates with learning rate 0.01, KL multiplier one, zero weight decay, no dropout, no centering and no extra structural penalties. Full batches retain source row order. The structural backbone options are disabled in the main comparison. Three initialization seeds (42, 123 and 456) are evaluated, without selecting the best seed. There is no test-driven hyperparameter search or early stopping.

The \textbf{fixed neural control} uses the same hidden architecture and budget with random terms removed. The \textbf{classical mixed baseline} uses the same fixed and random designs: Gaussian LMMs are fitted by ML using \texttt{lme4::lmer}; binomial GLMMs use \texttt{glmer} with the Laplace approximation \citep{bates2014fitting}. The binomial fitting routine tries \texttt{bobyqa}, then \texttt{nloptwrap} and \texttt{nlminbwrap} if an optimizer raises an error, retaining the first successful fit; test performance is not used to choose the optimizer. Known-group predictions include conditional fitted effects, whereas Regime B uses zero effects. Final optimizer convergence checks passed. On the primary split, only the Train random-intercept fits were singular, in both regimes. These boundary estimates are retained and reported; a fitted group-variance parameter need not be nonzero merely because a mixed model was specified.

\textbf{XGBoost} uses 200 trees, maximum depth 6 and learning rate 0.05 \citep{chen2016xgboost}. \textbf{Random Forest} uses 200 trees and minimum leaf size two. Both use seed 42. All methods receive the same substantive predictors; in Regime A, trees additionally receive training-fitted one-hot group indicators to make known-group information available. Trees receive no group indicators in Regime B. These are fixed comparator configurations, not exhaustively tuned methods.

\subsubsection{Metrics and Reproducibility}

Regression RMSE and MAE are reported in original outcome units after reversing training-target standardization; $R^2$ is also retained in the result files. Classification tables report AUROC and Brier score, with accuracy and log loss retained in those files. Lower Brier scores indicate smaller squared probability error; they alone do not establish calibration. Raw RMSE is not averaged across datasets with different units.

Neural entries in the primary tables are the mean and sample SD of metrics across three initialization seeds on the same test split. The sensitivity tables first average the metric over initialization seeds within each split, then report the mean and sample SD of these five split values. Repeated holdouts reuse observations and can repeat group partitions; these SDs describe sensitivity and are not standard errors. This SD does not estimate sampling uncertainty and is not a confidence interval. Classical and tree baselines use a single fit. No significance tests across datasets are claimed.

The executed environment used PyTorch 2.5.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1, XGBoost 3.2.0, R 4.4.1 and lme4 1.1-35.5. Scripts, versions, source checksums, per-seed metrics, baseline diagnostics and split manifests are provided in \texttt{experiments/}. The canonical suite is \texttt{run\_manuscript\_benchmarks.py}; tables are generated directly from its aggregate outputs. Source records and per-row predictions are cached locally and are not distributed with the manuscript.

\subsection{Results}

\subsubsection{Within-Group Regression}
TabMixNN has lower RMSE than the fixed neural control on all five known-group regression tasks, although the difference on Radon is small ($0.771$ vs $0.772$). The comparison with other methods is task-dependent. On MathAchieve, RMSE is $6.132$ for TabMixNN, $6.123$ for XGBoost and $6.059$ for the classical mixed model. On Spruce, TabMixNN ($0.148$) has lower RMSE than the fixed neural control ($0.658$) and the classical mixed model ($0.326$). ChickWeight also shows a large within-dataset difference from the fixed neural control ($5.580$ vs $40.278$ g). These comparisons support the use of fitted group information for these tasks, but do not isolate the contribution of each random-effect component.

\input{regression_A_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

\subsubsection{Out-of-Group Regression}
Without observed outcomes from the test groups, the advantage is smaller and more variable. On Radon, TabMixNN RMSE ($0.735$) is below XGBoost ($0.862$) and RF ($0.814$), while the classical mixed model is lower still ($0.711$). MathAchieve also shows TabMixNN ($6.235$) below XGBoost ($6.407$) and RF ($6.750$), with the classical mixed model lowest ($6.107$). On Spruce, neural and tree methods have RMSE near $0.61$, compared with $0.660$ for the classical mixed model; the known-group advantage of TabMixNN is absent. The contrast between Tables~\ref{tab:regression_A} and~\ref{tab:regression_B} shows why the two prediction settings must be reported separately.

\input{regression_B_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

\subsubsection{Within-Group Classification}
Known-group classification shows heterogeneous results. Toenail has the largest AUROC difference from the fixed neural control: $0.942 \pm 0.006$ vs $0.687 \pm 0.010$. VerbAgg and Train also show higher AUROC than the fixed neural control. Contraception and Exam show smaller differences, and the classical mixed model has higher AUROC than TabMixNN on both tasks. The ranking by AUROC need not match the ranking by Brier score, as illustrated by Contraception.

\input{classification_A_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

\subsubsection{Out-of-Group Classification}
For entirely unseen groups, Toenail shows a reversal: TabMixNN AUROC is $0.542 \pm 0.042$, while the fixed neural control and classical mixed model have AUROC $0.670$ and $0.681$, respectively. The known-group gain therefore does not carry over to this prediction setting. VerbAgg and Train retain higher TabMixNN AUROC than the fixed neural control ($0.697$ vs $0.679$ and $0.737$ vs $0.683$), although the classical mixed model has lower Brier scores on both tasks. On Exam, the classical mixed model has AUROC $0.815$, compared with $0.762$ for TabMixNN. These results do not identify which architectural or optimization difference explains the rankings.

\input{classification_B_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

\subsubsection{Linear Mixed-Model Check}
On Sleepstudy we additionally fit a scalar linear TabMixNN decoder using the same intercept/slope structure and split as the LMM. Regime-A RMSE is about 32.5 ms for linear VI and 32.2 ms for ML. This is a numerical check of predictions under a simple mean structure. It does not establish equality of variance estimates, posterior uncertainty or REML fitting, and it should not be extrapolated to the nonlinear benchmark model.

\input{linear_check_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

\subsubsection{Ablation Studies}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation_comprehensive} compares seven configurations on the same Sleepstudy observation holdout. Removing random effects increases error relative to the intercept/slope model. Adding static or dynamic latent structure does not show a uniform improvement across seeds, and the comparison does not identify an optimal architecture. The three-seed variability and fixed update budget should be considered when interpreting small differences. No general recommendation about layer count or learning rate is inferred from this single dataset.

\subsubsection{Sensitivity to the Data Split}
The five split values are an exploratory robustness check with the same fixed
training budget. They are neither five independent studies nor a substitute
for external validation. All twenty dataset/regime combinations have five
distinct test partitions. No favorable
split or initialization is selected for reporting.

\input{split_regression_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier
\input{split_classification_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

Across splits, TabMixNN retains lower mean RMSE than the fixed neural control
on all five known-group regression tasks. The Spruce difference remains large
($0.146 \pm 0.008$ vs fixed NN $0.649 \pm 0.008$), whereas the Radon
difference is smaller than the displayed three-decimal precision.
TabMixNN has lower five-split mean RMSE than XGBoost on four of five
known-group tasks and three of five unseen-group tasks. The classical mixed
model has lower mean RMSE than TabMixNN on three of five tasks in each regime.
On unseen-group Radon, for example, RMSE is $0.751 \pm 0.050$ for
TabMixNN, $0.890 \pm 0.068$ for XGBoost and $0.734 \pm 0.051$ for the
classical mixed model. These counts describe numerical rankings under the
fixed protocol; they do not establish statistically significant differences.

For classification, Toenail shows the largest and most consistent known-group
benefit ($0.951 \pm 0.014$ vs fixed NN $0.670 \pm 0.020$), but the
out-of-group reversal is also consistent ($0.591 \pm 0.068$ vs fixed NN
$0.682 \pm 0.024$). VerbAgg and Train retain higher TabMixNN mean AUROC
than the fixed neural control in both regimes.
TabMixNN has higher mean AUROC than XGBoost on three of five known-group
tasks and two of five unseen-group tasks. The classical mixed model has
higher mean AUROC than TabMixNN on all five unseen-group tasks, including
Exam ($0.797 \pm 0.013$ vs $0.749 \pm 0.013$). These comparisons
support task-specific predictive benefits, not a uniform advantage for unseen
groups.

\subsubsection{Probability Calibration Diagnostics}
Calibration is assessed on the primary held-out predictions, without modifying
them. A logistic model of observed outcome on predicted log-odds estimates an
intercept and slope jointly, with probabilities clipped to $[10^{-6},1-10^{-6}]$
only for that diagnostic transformation. The table averages coefficients over
three separate fitted seeds, rather than evaluating a probability ensemble.
Repeated observations are dependent, so independent-row standard errors are
not reported. Mean probability error and fixed-bin summaries are also retained
for all classification comparators in the reproducibility artifact. These
checks complement discrimination and squared probability error; they do not
establish transportable calibration.

\input{calibration_table.tex}
\FloatBarrier

All ten TabMixNN calibration slopes in Table~\ref{tab:calibration} are below
one, ranging from 0.082 to 0.731, indicating that the fitted log-odds are too
extreme under this diagnostic on the primary split. A mean probability close
to the observed event fraction does not resolve this problem: Exam in regime
A has a mean error of only $0.002$ but a slope of 0.684. On Toenail in regime
B, the observed event fraction is 0.202 and the mean predicted probability
is 0.045, an underprediction of 15.7 percentage points. These results limit
the use of the fitted probabilities as absolute risks, even where
discrimination is useful. They do not assess posterior predictive coverage.

\subsection{Interpretability Analysis}

Figures~\ref{fig:ablation_days_effects}--\ref{fig:ablation_breakdown} are descriptive plots from a separate fit to all 180 Sleepstudy observations (seed 42, 2,000 updates, the same nonlinear architecture). All training rows form the background. Values are transformed back to milliseconds. The fixed-design Days column is perturbed while random-slope values and group indices remain fixed, as described in Section~\ref{sec:interpretation}.

The fitted lines in Figure~\ref{fig:ablation_days_effects} summarize the plotted perturbations; they are neither random-slope coefficients nor causal effects of sleep deprivation. Figure~\ref{fig:ablation_subject_comparison} summarizes their distribution. Figure~\ref{fig:ablation_breakdown} displays the same column perturbation at three observed days; its bars are not an additive decomposition of a prediction. The complete generator is \texttt{create\_feature\_ablation\_plots.py} in the experiments directory.

\subsection{Scope of the Empirical Evidence}

These experiments evaluate Gaussian regression, binomial classification and one component comparison on ten grouped datasets. They do not evaluate survival prediction, multitask benefit, genomic prediction or the spatial manifold backbone. The repeated splits probe sensitivity to the held-out rows or groups, but the exploratory dataset selection and limited model configurations leave selection and tuning sensitivity unresolved. Specialized mixed-effects machine-learning baselines such as LMMNN and GPBoost are not evaluated. The package supports additional interfaces, but no performance claim for them follows from the present results.
